Applied economics · Firm-level evidence

How Canadian firms work: evidence from the 2024 Enterprise Survey

What holds Canadian businesses back, who innovates and exports, how firms finance themselves, and how this differs by size, sector, region and gender.

By Shadi Rahimfallah

This is an independent analysis. All analysis and interpretation are my own and are not affiliated with or endorsed by any company or organization, including the World Bank or any firm in the survey. Any errors are mine.

Data: World Bank Enterprise Survey, Canada 2024Formal private firms with 5+ employeesFieldwork April 2024 – April 2025
4parts
21sections
35further analyses
47figures
Part 1

Overview

What the survey is and the main messages.

1.1Key takeaways

  1. Skills are the top constraint. An inadequately educated workforce is named as the biggest obstacle more often than anything else, ahead of tax rates and political instability.
  2. Finance is not the bottleneck for most firms. Most firms that did not borrow say they did not need to; credit constraints are concentrated among small firms.
  3. Canada trades with one partner. The large majority of exporters sell mainly to the United States, which is also the main source of imported inputs.
  4. R&D is the common thread. Firms that spend on R&D are clearly more likely both to export and to innovate, after accounting for sector, region and size.
  5. Small firms carry the heaviest compliance load. Per worker, tax compliance takes far more time in small firms than in large ones.
  6. Regional gaps are small once industry mix is held constant. After sector and size controls, the provinces look very similar.

1.2What the survey covers

The Enterprise Survey interviews owners and managers of formal private firms about their day-to-day experience. For applied work, each question is a statistic about the business economy: a share of firms, a distribution, an average percentage, or a typical amount of time or money. Grouped by subject, the questions cover six areas of the economy.

Several topics cut across these areas: gender (ownership, management, workforce, training), the state (government ownership, contracts, inspections, state banks), formality and informality (informal competitors, informal payments), resources and utilities (energy, water, land, materials) and foreign links (ownership, licensed technology, exports, imported inputs). Results can be broken down by firm size, eight sectors, five regions and four city sizes.

Part 2

Descriptive findings

Weighted shares of Canadian firms by size, sector and region.

2.1What holds firms back

Firms picked the single biggest obstacle to their operations from fifteen options, and separately rated each one from “no obstacle” to “very severe”.

The skills gap is felt across all sizes. Access to finance and the cost of hiring weigh more on small firms, while large firms point more often to tax rates.

2.2Innovation and R&D

Innovation means introducing a new or significantly improved product or process in the last three years. R&D covers in-house or contracted research, excluding market research.

Innovation is spread across firm sizes, but R&D spending rises sharply with size.

2.3Trade

Manufacturing sectors and professional services are the most export-oriented. On both sides of trade the United States dominates, which makes Canadian firms highly exposed to U.S. trade policy.

2.4Finance

Most firms finance working capital internally. Credit constraints are rare overall but more common among small firms, which also rate access to finance as a bigger obstacle.

2.5Gender

Women’s participation is highest in food and retail and lowest in fabricated metal. The gap between ownership and management is widest in food and professional services.

2.6Regions and infrastructure

Central Canada leads on R&D, credit, training and emissions monitoring; British Columbia on exporting; Atlantic Canada on innovation but also on outages and skills shortages.

2.7Green economy

Green practices rise steadily with firm size. Energy management is far more common than CO₂ monitoring, which remains a minority practice even among large firms.

2.8What goes together

Exporting, innovating and productivity are regressed on firm characteristics with sector and region controls, survey weights and robust standard errors. Blue dots have 95% intervals that exclude zero.

Exporters are more often foreign-owned, certified and R&D-active. Innovation goes with R&D and with a credit line. Older, multi-site firms and firms with a website report higher sales per worker. Women-led firms report lower sales per worker within the same sector and region, an association that may reflect differences in activity within sectors.

The survey is a single cross-section, so these are associations, not causal effects.

Part 3

Further analyses

Thirty-five applied-economics analyses, grouped by topic. Each states the question, the finding, a figure and the method.

3.1Innovation

What drives innovation and R&D, and whether they pay off.

A01Regression

What makes a Canadian firm innovate?

Which firm traits go with introducing new products or processes?

R&D and credit go with innovation.

Spending on R&D and having a bank loan or credit line are the clearest correlates of both new products and new processes. Women-led and larger firms are slightly less likely to report new products, while foreign ownership, exporting, certification and training show no clear link once these are held constant. The two kinds of innovation are only weakly related to each other.

Method and data
Method
Probit or logit with survey weights, sector and region fixed effects; report average marginal effects. Run product and process innovation separately, then a bivariate probit to let the two decisions be correlated.
Questions used
h1 h5 l1 b5 b2b d3c h8 l10 k82 b7 b7a b8 c22b e6
Watch out
Cross-section: innovation and R&D are chosen together, so read effects as associations.
A02Advanced

Innovation and productivity: the CDM chain

Does R&D lead to innovation, and does innovation raise productivity?

The R&D → innovation → productivity chain is weak in Canada’s data.

Larger firms and exporters are much more likely to do R&D. But in the next steps, predicted R&D does not significantly raise the chance of innovating, and predicted innovation does not significantly raise sales per worker. Among R&D performers, foreign-owned firms spend more relative to sales.

Method and data
Method
Crépon–Duguet–Mairesse model in three steps: (1) Heckman selection for whether and how much a firm spends on R&D (h8, h9/sales); (2) probit of innovation on predicted R&D intensity; (3) OLS of log sales per worker on predicted innovation.
Questions used
h8 h9 h1 h5 d2 l1 b2b d3c k82 e2b l10
Watch out
Needs exclusion restrictions in step 1; R&D amounts (h9) are answered by fewer firms.
A03Regression

Does competition push or block innovation?

Is there an inverted-U between competition and innovation?

No inverted U between competition and innovation.

Neither the number of competitors nor its square is statistically significant, so the data do not support the inverted-U pattern found elsewhere. Firms that face informal competitors are somewhat more likely to innovate, but only at the margin of significance.

Method and data
Method
Logit of innovation on number of competitors and its square (Aghion et al. 2005), plus pricing power (e33) and informal competition (e11). Plot predicted probability against competitors.
Questions used
h1 h5 e2b e32 e33 e11 e1
Watch out
Competitor counts are self-reported and top-coded answers are common; consider log or categories.
A04Regression

Foreign technology and in-house R&D: substitutes or complements?

Do firms that license foreign technology do more or less of their own R&D?

Foreign technology neither replaces nor clearly complements own R&D.

Licensing foreign technology has no significant link with doing R&D, for domestic or foreign-owned firms. Exporting is the strong correlate of R&D. The joint model finds no significant correlation between licensing and R&D decisions.

Method and data
Method
Probit of R&D on foreign licence and interaction with foreign ownership; or bivariate probit of R&D and licensing.
Questions used
h8 e6 b2b d12b d3c l1
Watch out
Small number of licensing firms in some sectors.

3.2Productivity & growth

Who is productive, who grows, and why.

A05Regression

Exporter productivity premium

Are exporters more productive, and where in the distribution is the gap largest?

The exporter premium sits at the top of the distribution.

On average, exporters are not significantly more productive once foreign ownership, certification and R&D are controlled, and matching estimates are close to zero. Quantile regressions show why: the premium is not significant in the lower part of the distribution, then becomes significant from the median and is largest among the most productive firms.

Method and data
Method
OLS and quantile regressions (10th, 50th, 90th percentiles) of log sales per worker on an exporter dummy; propensity-score matching as a robustness check.
Questions used
d2 l1 d3b d3c b2b b5 b8 h8 a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Self-selection: productive firms start exporting, so this is not the effect of exporting itself.
A06Advanced

Total factor productivity in manufacturing

How productive are manufacturing firms once capital and materials are accounted for?

Manufacturing output is driven by labour; TFP has no clear correlates.

In a Cobb-Douglas production function, the labour elasticity dominates, materials matter less and capital is close to zero, with roughly constant returns to scale. Productivity (TFP) is not linked to foreign ownership, exporting, R&D or age in this small manufacturing sample; training shows only a borderline negative association.

Method and data
Method
Estimate a Cobb-Douglas (log sales on log labour cost, log materials, log capital replacement value) by sub-sector; keep the residual as TFP; then relate TFP to ownership, management and exporting.
Questions used
d2 n2a n2e n7a l1 f1
Watch out
Manufacturing sub-sample only; capital is replacement value, not book value.
A07Regression

Does firm growth depend on size? (Gibrat’s law)

Do small firms grow faster than large ones?

Small and young firms grow faster: Gibrat’s law fails.

Firms that were smaller two years earlier grew faster in both employment and sales, and younger firms grew faster than older ones. Having a loan or credit line goes with faster growth (significant for employment, borderline for sales). Employment growth is highest among the youngest firms and lowest among the oldest.

Method and data
Method
Regress annualized employment growth (l1 vs l2) and sales growth (d2 vs n3) on log initial size and firm age; test whether the size coefficient is zero.
Questions used
l1 l2 d2 n3 b5 k82 h1 d3c a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Only surviving firms are observed (survivor bias); sales growth is nominal.
A08Regression

Management practices and performance

Do better-managed firms have higher productivity?

Better management goes with higher productivity, at the margin.

A higher structured-management score is associated with higher sales per worker, though only at the edge of statistical significance. Firms where the owner is also the top manager score somewhat lower on management, at the margin of significance. Large firms have the highest average scores.

Method and data
Method
Build a management score as the average of standardized r1–r11 answers (World Management Survey style), then regress log productivity on the score with controls.
Questions used
d2 l1 r1 r2 r3 r4 r5 r6 r7 r8 r9 r10 r11 b3a b7
Watch out
Asked of a sub-sample; reverse causality (profitable firms adopt practices).
A09Descriptive

Firm life cycle: how much do firms grow after birth?

How large are mature firms compared with their size at start-up?

Canadian firms grow slowly over their life cycle.

The typical young firm is barely larger than at start-up. Even firms more than forty years old are, at the median, only a few times their initial size. Long-lived firms in professional services and manufacturing have grown the most; retail and hotels the least.

Method and data
Method
Compare current employment with employment at start (b6) by age cohort; average growth multiple by sector (Hsieh–Klenow life-cycle comparison).
Questions used
l1 b6 b5 b6b a4a
Watch out
Recall error for older firms’ start-up size.

3.3Finance

Access to credit, financing structure and payments.

A10Regression

Who is credit constrained?

Which firms are turned down or discouraged from borrowing?

Credit constraints are rare and not concentrated in one firm type.

Few firms are credit constrained, and no single trait predicts it strongly. Innovators and firms with audited accounts are slightly more likely to be constrained, but only at the margin. Among discouraged borrowers, unfavourable interest rates and expected rejection are the main reasons.

Method and data
Method
Build a constrained indicator (rejected, or did not apply for reasons other than enough capital), then probit. Separate discouraged borrowers from rejected ones.
Questions used
k162 k17 k20a1 l1 b5 k21 b4 b2b d3c h1 a3 a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Few constrained firms in Canada, so groups get small fast.
A11Advanced

Gender gap in access to finance

Do women-owned or women-led firms get credit on different terms?

No gender gap in access to credit.

Women-owned and women-led firms are as likely as others to have a loan or credit line. The decomposition finds no total gap, and nothing explained or unexplained. Female owners are no more likely to pledge personal assets or to be discouraged from applying.

Method and data
Method
Probit for having a loan; OLS of collateral value relative to loan size (k15a/k11); Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition to split the gap into explained (firm traits) and unexplained parts.
Questions used
k82 k14a k14d k15a k17 b4 b4a b7a l1 b5 k21 a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Collateral items are answered only by borrowers.
A12Regression

How firms finance working capital and investment

How do funding mixes differ by size and age?

Firms fund themselves mainly from internal cash.

Internal funds dominate working capital in every size class. The bank share rises with firm size and with audited accounts, while foreign-owned firms rely less on internal funds and slightly more on non-bank lenders.

Method and data
Method
Fractional logit (Papke–Wooldridge) for each share; or describe the mix by size class.
Questions used
k3a k3bc k3e k3f k5a k5bc k5i l1 b5 k21 b2b
Watch out
Investment shares exist only for firms that bought fixed assets.
A13Regression

Digital payments and fintech adoption

Which firms take most of their payments electronically, and what does it cost them?

Online presence goes with digital payments.

Electronic payments are widespread in every sector. Firms with a website or social-media page receive a much larger share of payments electronically, and older firms a smaller share. Typical fees are low and money usually arrives within a day or two.

Method and data
Method
Fractional logit for e-payment shares; describe fees and settlement days by sector.
Questions used
k33 k38 k342 k36 k35 l1 a4a c22b a3
Watch out
Fee questions are answered by e-payment users only.

3.4Labour & gender

Workforce, skills, training and gender gaps.

A14Regression

Female leadership and female employment

Do firms led or owned by women employ more women?

Women-led firms employ more women.

Firms with a female top manager have a markedly higher share of women in their full-time workforce; female ownership has a smaller positive link. Firm size and age make no difference.

Method and data
Method
Fractional logit of the female share of full-time workers (l5/l1) on female top manager and ownership, with sector fixed effects.
Questions used
l5 l1 b7a b4 b4a a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Sorting: women managers may be concentrated in sectors that hire more women.
A15Advanced

Gender gap in firm performance

Do women-led firms differ in productivity and growth, and why?

A large productivity gap that firm traits do not explain.

Women-led firms report substantially lower sales per worker. Almost none of this gap is explained by size, age, manager experience, finance, trade, sector or region, so it is mostly unexplained. Sales per worker does not capture differences in activity within sectors, hours worked or profits, so this is not evidence of lower efficiency.

Method and data
Method
Oaxaca–Blinder decomposition of log sales per worker between female- and male-led firms; check sector composition within 8 sectors.
Questions used
d2 l1 b7a b4 b7 b5 k82 a4a a6a
Watch out
Association only; sales per worker penalizes labour-intensive sectors.
A16Regression

Skills shortage as an obstacle

Which firms see an inadequately educated workforce as a severe obstacle?

Innovators feel the skills gap most.

Firms that innovate are significantly more likely to rate an inadequately educated workforce as a major obstacle. Workforce education, training, size and city size are not significant. Firms in Atlantic Canada, the Prairies and the North report skills problems more often than firms in Central Canada.

Method and data
Method
Ordered probit of the 0–4 rating; compare with the share naming it the biggest obstacle (m1a).
Questions used
l30b l9b l10 h1 l1 a3 a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Perception data; firms in tight labour markets may rate it higher.
A17Regression

Who trains workers?

What explains formal training?

Large, R&D-active and foreign-owned firms train.

Foreign ownership, R&D and size are strongly linked with offering formal training. Among firms that train, women-led firms train a somewhat larger share of their female workers, at the margin of significance.

Method and data
Method
Probit for offering training; fractional models for the share of workers trained, including female workers (l12a).
Questions used
l10 l11a l11b l12a l1 h1 h8 b2b l30b l9b
Watch out
Training share items have sub-sample answers.
A18Descriptive

Labour flexibility: temporary workers, dismissal and severance

How costly is adjusting the workforce?

Temporary work is concentrated in seasonal sectors.

Hotels and restaurants, food, manufacturing and construction use temporary workers the most; retail and fabricated metal the least. Severance and dismissal times are modest and do not differ clearly across provinces. Firms that dismissed workers are more likely to see labour regulation as a major obstacle.

Method and data
Method
Describe weeks to dismiss and weeks of severance by region (provincial labour codes differ); relate to the labour-regulation obstacle with an ordered probit.
Questions used
l6 l35 l36 l30a l1 a2 a4a l37
Watch out
Only firms that dismissed workers answer dismissal time.

3.5Trade

Exporting, trade partners and border costs.

A19Regression

Who exports, and how much?

What determines entry into exporting and export intensity?

Capabilities, not size, decide who exports.

Foreign ownership, R&D, quality certification and licensed foreign technology all raise the chance of exporting, while size does not once these are included. Among exporters, larger firms export a bigger share of their sales.

Method and data
Method
Two-part model or Heckman selection: probit for exporting (10%+ of sales), then a fractional model or OLS for the export share among exporters.
Questions used
d3b d3c l1 b2b b8 h8 h1 b5 e6 a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Needs an exclusion restriction for Heckman; two-part model avoids it.
A20Descriptive

Dependence on the United States

How concentrated are Canadian firms’ trade partners?

Most exporters depend on the U.S. and the land border.

In every province with enough exporters, most sell mainly to the United States, and the large majority of direct exporters ship through a land border. Atlantic exporters are the exception, with more diverse destinations, though their sample is small.

Method and data
Method
Tabulate main destination and origin by sector and region; compare land, sea and air exit points.
Questions used
d31x d38x a4a a2 d32 d39
Watch out
Only the main partner is recorded, not the full mix.
A21Descriptive

Border frictions and trade costs

How long and how costly are customs and border procedures?

Imports face more border friction than exports.

Imported goods take longer than exports to clear customs and all border procedures, and compliance costs are higher for imports. Shipments through seaports and airports take longer than those crossing land borders.

Method and data
Method
Weighted medians by exit/entry point and firm size; regressions of days on firm traits; tobit for cost shares at zero.
Questions used
d4a d33a d342 d14a d40a d412 d32 d39 l1 a4a
Watch out
Small numbers of direct traders in some cells.
A22Regression

Imported inputs and productivity

Are firms using foreign inputs more productive?

Imported inputs go with higher productivity.

Firms that import directly and firms using more foreign inputs have significantly higher sales per worker. Exporting adds no further premium once importing is accounted for, and two-way traders show no extra gain.

Method and data
Method
OLS of log productivity on foreign-input share and direct importing; test two-way traders (import and export).
Questions used
d2 l1 d12b d13 d3c b2b a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Selection into importing.

3.6Infrastructure & green

Utilities, digital adoption and climate.

A23Regression

Cost of power and internet disruptions

How much do outages cost firms, and where?

Power outages: similar across provinces, worse in the North and possibly in small towns.

Outage rates are similar in the four main regions, while the territories are a clear outlier. Firms in towns under 50,000 are more likely to experience outages and report somewhat larger losses, at the margin of significance.

Method and data
Method
Probit for experiencing outages by region and city size; tobit for losses as % of sales (many zeros).
Questions used
c6 c7 c8a c9a c39 c40a c41a a2 a3 a4a c10
Watch out
Loss figures are firm estimates.
A24Regression

Digital adoption

Which firms are digitally connected, and does it pay?

Digital adoption is widespread.

Most firms have a website, file taxes online and handle most payments electronically. Larger and younger firms are more digital, and exporters slightly less. The digital index is not linked with sales growth.

Method and data
Method
Build a digital index (website, e-payment share, broadband); regress on firm traits, then relate to sales growth.
Questions used
c22b k33 c36 l1 b5 b7 a3 a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Website ownership is near universal, so variation is limited.
A25Regression

Green practices: who adopts them?

What drives CO2 monitoring and energy-management measures?

Certification drives green practices.

Firms with an international quality certification are much more likely both to monitor CO₂ and to adopt energy-management measures, and both rise with size. The two practices go strongly together. Firms with a higher energy-cost share are less likely to monitor CO₂ and no more likely to manage energy, and past weather damage shows no link.

Method and data
Method
Bivariate probit of the two practices; include energy cost share (n2b/d2) and past weather damage (ge3).
Questions used
ge7 ge8d l1 d3c b2b n2b d2 ge3 b8 a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Self-reported adoption.
A26Descriptive

Climate exposure

Which firms suffered extreme-weather damage, and how much?

Climate damage is rare but uneven.

Few firms report assets damaged by extreme weather in the last three years. The territories and Atlantic Canada report it most often and British Columbia least. Where damage occurs, it is typically small relative to sales.

Method and data
Method
Probit of damage by region and sector; describe damage relative to sales.
Questions used
ge3 ge3a a2 a3 a4a g6b
Watch out
Rare event: few firms report damage.

3.7Government & institutions

Regulation, contracts, informality and perceptions.

A27Regression

Regulatory burden by firm size

Is regulation a heavier burden for small firms?

Tax compliance is a fixed cost that weighs on small firms.

Larger firms spend more total hours on taxes and are inspected more often, but per worker the burden falls sharply with size: small firms spend several times more tax hours per employee than large firms. Outsourcing tax work does not reduce reported hours.

Method and data
Method
OLS of management time on regulation and hours on taxes, scaled per worker, on log size; check if outsourcing tax work (j34) changes the burden.
Questions used
j2 j35 j3 l1 j34 j36 a2 a4a a6a
Watch out
Perception of time is approximate.
A28Regression

Who wins government contracts?

Which firms bid for and secure public contracts, and how slow is payment?

Larger and audited firms bid for public contracts.

Firm size and audited accounts are linked with bidding for or securing government contracts. Women-owned and women-led firms are not significantly different. Roughly half of contract holders find tender requirements difficult, and payment typically takes about a month.

Method and data
Method
Probit for bidding or winning; describe payment days and tender difficulty by size.
Questions used
j6a j42 j43 j41 l1 b4 b7a b2b a2 a4a a6a
Watch out
Small number of contract holders.
A29Regression

Competition from informal firms

Which formal firms face unregistered competitors, and does it hurt them?

Informal competition is felt in food and professional services.

Competition from unregistered firms is reported most often in food, professional services, construction and hotels. Facing informal competitors has no significant link with innovation or sales growth.

Method and data
Method
Probit of facing informal competition; then include it as a driver in innovation or growth regressions.
Questions used
e11 e30 a4a a3 a2 l1
Watch out
Perception-based.
A30Regression

Perceptions versus experience

Do firms that call electricity, crime or courts an obstacle actually experience more problems?

Electricity ratings track experience; corruption ratings do not.

Firms with more outages are much more likely to call electricity a major obstacle. Court ratings are related to having a commercial dispute only at the margin of significance. The small number of firms that report informal payments are significantly less likely to rate corruption a major obstacle.

Method and data
Method
Cross-tabulate ratings against objective experience (e.g. c30a against outages c6/c7); ordered probit of each rating on the matching experience variable.
Questions used
c30a i30 h30 j30f c6 c7 o1 j7a j5
Watch out
Rating scale may be used differently across firms.
A31Advanced

Mapping the business environment

Which obstacles move together?

Sixteen obstacles reduce to four business-environment factors.

Factor analysis groups the obstacle ratings into tax and governance, markets and finance, infrastructure and order, and the labour market. Atlantic Canada scores worst on tax and governance, the territories and British Columbia on infrastructure and order, and the territories and the Prairies on the labour market.

Method and data
Method
Principal component or factor analysis of all 0–4 ratings to build indices (tax/regulation, infrastructure, labour); compare index scores across regions and sectors.
Questions used
j30a j30b j30c j30e j30f h30 i30 l30a l30b l30c k30 c30a d30a d30b g30a e30 a2 a4a a6a
Watch out
Ratings are ordinal; use polychoric correlations if possible.

3.8Ownership & location

Foreign and owner-managed firms, regions and cities.

A32Advanced

Foreign-owned firms in Canada

How do foreign-owned firms differ in productivity, exporting, training and certification?

Foreign-owned firms are more global and more formal, not more productive.

Compared with similar domestic firms, foreign-owned firms are far more likely to hold a quality certification and to export, and (by weighting, though not by nearest-neighbour matching) to train their workers. They are no more likely to do R&D or innovate, and their sales per worker is not significantly different.

Method and data
Method
Propensity-score matching or inverse-probability weighting of foreign (10%+) vs domestic firms on size, age, sector and region.
Questions used
d2 d3c l10 b8 b2b l1 b5 a4a a2 a6a
Watch out
Few foreign firms in small cells.
A33Regression

Owner-managed versus professionally managed firms

Do firms where the main owner is the top manager behave differently?

Owner-managers borrow more but manage less formally.

Firms run by their main owner are significantly more likely to have a loan or credit line, and score lower on structured management at the margin. They do not differ in productivity, innovation, training or growth.

Method and data
Method
Compare management, innovation and finance outcomes by b3a and legal form (b1) with controls.
Questions used
r1 h1 k82 d2 b3a b1 b7 l1
Watch out
Management items are sub-sample only.
A34Descriptive

Regional economies of Canada

How do firms in the Atlantic, Central, Prairies, BC and the North differ?

After sector and size controls, the provinces barely differ.

The raw regional differences seen earlier largely disappear once sector and size are held constant: the provinces do not differ significantly from Central Canada on exporting, innovation, credit or training. The one clear provincial difference is less R&D in the Prairies. The territories differ more, but their sample is very small.

Method and data
Method
Weighted indicator tables by region, then regressions with region fixed effects to see which differences survive sector and size controls.
Questions used
d2 d3c h1 k82 l30b c6 a2 a3 a4a a6a
Watch out
The North has very few firms; pool or report with a warning.
A35Regression

Urban premium

Are firms in big cities more productive and innovative than small-town firms?

Big-city firms innovate more but are not more productive.

Firms in cities over one million people are more likely to innovate than firms in small towns. There is no significant urban premium in sales per worker or in exporting.

Method and data
Method
OLS of log productivity on city-size categories (a3) with sector and region controls.
Questions used
d2 l1 h1 a3 a3c a2 a4a
Watch out
City size is grouped into four bands.

Part 4

Data and method

4.1Data, weights and definitions

  • Data. World Bank Enterprise Survey, Canada 2024 (fieldwork April 2024 – April 2025): formal private firms with five or more employees in manufacturing and services, stratified by sector, size and region.
  • Weights. All figures use the survey’s median-eligibility weights, so they describe the population of eligible Canadian firms; variance estimates account for the stratified design. The quantile regressions in analysis A05 are unweighted.
  • Groups. Size: small 5–19, medium 20–99, large 100+ employees. Regions: Atlantic, Central (Ontario and Quebec), Prairies, British Columbia, and the territories, whose sample is very small.
  • Definitions. Exporter: direct plus indirect exports at least 10% of sales. Major obstacle: rated “major” or “very severe”. “Don’t know” and refusals are excluded.
  • Interpretation. One cross-section of self-reported answers; results are associations. With many models, a few borderline results may arise by chance, so the clearly significant ones deserve the most weight.

The firm-level data are licensed by the World Bank and are not reproduced or redistributed on this page. Figures show weighted aggregate estimates only. Researchers can request the data from the Enterprise Surveys Data Portal.
